Marburg
mar'boorg
n. (Hessian town on the Lahn; seat of the first Protestant university, of the colloquy of 1529, and of the Reformed reform of 1605)
German Marburg, from Mark, a boundary, and Burg, a fortified place—the border castle above the Lahn.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Marburg holds three places in the history of the Reformation. In 1527 Landgrave Philip of Hesse founded there the first university established as a Protestant foundation, which trained the ministry of Hesse and of much of central Germany. In October 1529 the same prince brought Luther and Zwingli, with Melanchthon, Bucer, Oecolampadius and others, to his castle to settle the quarrel over the Lord's Supper; they agreed on fourteen articles and parted on the fifteenth, and the Protestant division dates from that room. Then in 1605 Landgrave Moritz the Learned, having concluded that the Reformed doctrine was the biblical one, imposed on Hesse-Kassel the measures called the points of improvement: the images taken out of the churches, the Decalogue restored to its Reformed numbering so that the second commandment stood alone, and the bread broken in the Supper. The Lutheran professors of Marburg refused, were removed, and went to found Giessen, so that one Hessian university became two confessions. The dictionary enters Marburg because all three of its episodes are about the same thing: whether the plain words of Scripture govern the church's worship, and what it costs when two parties both answer yes and disagree about what the words say.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a colloquy as a conference, a mutual discourse; a university as a corporation for instruction in all the branches of learning; and improvement as advancement in anything good.

expand to see more

COLLOQUY, n. [L. colloquium.] Conversation; mutual discourse of two or more; conference; a dialogue.

UNIVERSITY, n. An assemblage of colleges established in any place, with professors for instructing students in the sciences and other branches of learning.

IMPROVEMENT, n. Advancement in any thing good or valuable; a making or growing better; the act of amending.

ARTICLE, n. A single clause in a contract or system of regulations; a point of faith distinctly stated.

DIVISION, n. [L. divisio.] The act of dividing; the state of being divided; discord; variance; disagreement.

Modern Corruption

Hessian town of the first Protestant university, of the 1529 colloquy on the Supper, and of the Reformed points of improvement of 1605.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The genuine controversy is the fifteenth article, and the dictionary states its position rather than lamenting the division. On the Supper it holds, with the Reformed, that the bread and wine are a sign and seal in which Christ is truly present to the believer by faith and by the Spirit, and it rejects transubstantiation, the Lutheran sacramental union, and the bare memorialism which denies the spiritual presence. The Marburg parting was therefore not a failure of charity on either side but a real difference about the nature of a sacrament, and it could not have been papered over.

The principle to recover is the second commandment in its own right. “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image” (Exo 20:4) stands as a separate commandment and is not a clause of the first; the medieval numbering which folded it into the first and split the tenth is the numbering under which the churches filled with images. Moritz's restoring of the Reformed order in 1605 was right, and the manner—a prince imposing a confession on professors and parishes—was the standing fault of the German second reformations.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek koinonia (G2842), communion, a sharing in common; Hebrew pesel (H6459), a graven image.

expand to see more

Greek koinonia (G2842) — fellowship, a having in common; “the communion of the blood of Christ”, 1 Corinthians 10:16.

Greek klao (G2806) — to break, as bread; “The bread which we break”, 1 Corinthians 10:16.

Hebrew pesel (H6459) — a graven or carved image; “any graven image, or any likeness”, Exodus 20:4.

Hebrew torah (H8451) — law, instruction; “To the law and to the testimony”, Isaiah 8:20.

Greek aletheia (G225) — truth; “the truth of the gospel”, Galatians 2:5.

Usage

"“The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?” (1Co 10:16) — the fifteenth article, October 1529."

"“Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image” (Exo 20:4) — the points of improvement of 1605, and the Reformed numbering restored."

"“To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) — the Lutheran professors removed, and Giessen founded."
